videos.title: Who Bought All the RAM in 2026? 🧠
videos.description:
Why are phones and laptops getting more expensive in 2026? The AI memory shortage, explained.
RAM (DRAM) prices are surging as AI data centres buy up memory.

TrendForce says DRAM contract prices rose about 80% in Q2 2026 and about 40% in Q3, with roughly 20% more forecast for Q4 — about three times the start-of-year level if that holds. videos.title: The Coin That Trapped Coca-Cola 🥤
videos.description:
Why did a Coke cost 5 cents for 70 years? The nickel Coke, explained.
How a 1899 bottling deal and nickel-only vending machines froze Coca-Cola's price.

In 1899 two lawyers got Coke's bottling rights with the syrup price fixed permanently. Coke tied its brand to five cents, and its vending machines took a single nickel — the next coin up, a dime, would have doubled the price. Coca-Cola asked the US Treasury for a 7.5-cent coin, and its boss even raised it with his hunting buddy, President Eisenhower. The answer was no. Inflation won, and the nickel Coke was gone by 1959.

videos.description:
Fake FBI "recovery" calls: why scam victims get scammed a second time.
How the IC3 impersonation / fund-recovery scam works, and the one rule that stops it.

After a scam, a second call comes: someone posing as the FBI or its Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) says they can get your money back for a small upfront fee. The FTC warns that recovery scammers buy lists of people who've already been scammed. The FBI (PSA, July 2026) warns of AI deepfake videos of an FBI leader sending victims to a spoofed IC3 site. The real IC3 never contacts you first and never asks for payment to recover lost funds.

videos.title: De Beers' $6.8B Problem 💎
videos.description:
"A Diamond Is Forever": how De Beers made diamonds feel rare, and why lab-grown diamonds are breaking the spell.
Why diamonds resell for so little, explained.

De Beers once controlled most of the world's diamond supply. In 1947 its ad agency, N.W. Ayer, wrote "A Diamond Is Forever" — and "forever" discouraged resale, so few people learned how little a used diamond fetches. Later ads pushed "two months' salary"; the share of US brides with a diamond ring rose from about 10% to about 80% (Al Jazeera). Lab-grown stones now cost up to 80–90% less, and Anglo American has written De Beers down by $6.8 billion since 2023.

videos.title: Someone Bought the Eiffel Tower? 🗼
videos.description:
The man who sold the Eiffel Tower: Victor Lustig's 1925 con, explained.
How a fake government letterhead and a luxury hotel fooled a Paris scrap dealer.

The Eiffel Tower was built on a 20-year permit. In 1925, con man Victor Lustig posed as a government official, invited scrap-metal dealers to the Hôtel de Crillon and said the state would secretly sell the tower for scrap. Dealer André Poisson paid, plus a bribe, and Lustig vanished. Poisson was too embarrassed to go to the police, so Lustig tried the same con again — this time a dealer called the police and he fled. Parts of the story come from later retellings.

videos.title: Stolen in 2017… With a Wheelbarrow? 🪙
videos.description:
The Big Maple Leaf: a 100 kg gold coin stolen from Berlin's Bode Museum with a wheelbarrow, and why its "$1 million" face value was the least valuable thing about it.

In March 2017, thieves climbed in from the railway tracks beside Berlin's Bode Museum and took the Big Maple Leaf, a 100 kg coin of 99.999% gold made by the Royal Canadian Mint. Its face value: one million Canadian dollars. Police put the gold at over $4 million at the time. Investigators believe it was cut up, melted and sold; three men were convicted in 2020 and the coin was never found. At gold's November 2026 price, 100 kg is worth about $13 million.

videos.title: Why Your Eggs Cost More Than Mine 🥚
videos.description:
Dynamic pricing explained: why the same eggs in the same store can show five different prices.
Personalised and algorithmic pricing: Instacart's price tests and AI airline fares.

Consumer Reports, Groundwork Collaborative and More Perfect Union found that Instacart showed nearly three in four grocery items at more than one price in an experiment; a dozen Lucerne eggs from one Safeway in Washington, D.C. showed $3.99, $4.28, $4.59, $4.69 or $4.79. Instacart ended its item price tests on 22 Dec 2025. Delta has said AI helps set fares on about 3% of its domestic flights, with plans for up to 20%; Delta says it doesn't target individuals with personalised fares. Before a big purchase, compare the price on another app, device or in the store.

videos.title: The Free Trial Trap 💳
videos.description:
Free trial auto-renew: why a "free" trial needs your card, and how companies profit when you forget to cancel.
Subscription traps, hard-to-find cancel buttons, and the Amazon Prime "Iliad" case.

When a free trial ends, the card on file is charged and the plan renews automatically. The US Federal Trade Commission accused Amazon of enrolling people in Prime without clear consent and making cancellation hard; internally the cancel flow was nicknamed "Iliad". Amazon denied wrongdoing but in September 2025 agreed to pay $2.5 billion to settle — a $1 billion civil penalty and $1.5 billion in customer refunds. The fix: set a reminder the day you sign up, and check your statement for charges you don't recognise. Not financial advice.

videos.title: The Job That Pays You… Then Robs You 💸
videos.description:
Task scam explained: the "get paid to like videos" job that ends with you paying them.
How app-optimisation and product-boosting job scams work, and the one rule that beats them.

It starts with an unexpected text or WhatsApp message. You like videos or rate products in sets of 40, an app shows your earnings climbing, and small early payouts make it feel real. Then a "double task" asks you to deposit your own money, usually in crypto, to unlock your earnings. The balance was never real. The FTC counted about 5,000 task-scam reports in all of 2023 and about 20,000 in just the first half of 2024. BBB Scam Tracker puts the median task-scam loss in 2025 at about $2,300. The FTC's rule: never pay to get paid.

videos.title: Why America Killed the Penny 🪙
videos.description:
Why the US stopped making the penny: each one-cent coin cost almost 4 cents to make.
The end of the US penny, and why the nickel loses money too.

In 2024 the US Mint spent about 3.69 cents to make each penny. Pennies had been made since 1793. The Treasury placed its final order for penny blanks in 2025, and the last circulating pennies were struck in Philadelphia on 12 Nov 2025. The nickel costs about 13.78 cents to make and is still being produced. More than 114 billion pennies are still in circulation, and they remain legal tender.

videos.description:
Fake FTC call scam: "Your phone number is linked to a crime and will be deactivated."
How the government-impersonation call moves you from a fake official to a fake police officer to a "security deposit".

On 22 Oct 2026 the US Federal Trade Commission warned about callers posing as FTC officials who say a phone in your name is running scams overseas. They read a fake badge ID, threaten to deactivate your number, transfer you to a fake police officer, ask for your ID and secrecy, then claim you're under arrest unless you pay a "security deposit". The FTC says real employees never ask for money, threats to disconnect your phone are a scam, and requests for secrecy are always a scam. Report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

videos.description:
Are Black Friday deals real? Why most "discounts" are the same price you could pay any other time.
The "was" price trick, countdown clocks, and why prices often drop again after the sale.

Consumer group Which? tracked 175 products at eight big UK retailers from May 2024 to May 2025. 83% were the same price or cheaper at least once outside the Black Friday sale period. videos.title: Infinite Money at the Bottom of the Sea 🌊
videos.description:
Rai stones of Yap: the giant stone money that worked even after one sank to the bottom of the sea.
How stone money on Yap shows what money really is.

On the Pacific island of Yap, money took the form of rai — huge carved stone discs, the largest about 3.6 metres wide and around 4 tonnes. Most were quarried on Palau, roughly 400 km away, and brought back by sea. Big stones were rarely moved; ownership changed by everyone agreeing who owned them. One stone sank on the way home, and the islanders still treated it as existing and kept trading it. Today most of our money is also just numbers that everyone agrees on.

videos.title: How Newton Lost His Fortune! 📉
videos.description:
Isaac Newton and the South Sea Bubble of 1720: how the genius behind gravity lost money in a stock bubble.
Why even smart investors buy at the top.

South Sea Company shares rose from about £130 in January 1720 to over £1,000 by June. Newton sold most of his shares early at a profit, then bought back in at roughly double the price before the crash. Estimates of his loss range from about £10,000 to over £20,000, and historians still debate the evidence. The famous line about calculating the stars but not the madness of people is attributed to him but not confirmed. Not financial advice.

Fake payment screenshot scam: how a "Payment successful" screen can show a green tick when no money was sent.
How shopkeepers get fooled by fake UPI/payment apps, and the one check that stops it.

The Mali emperor's pilgrimage to Mecca and its effect on Cairo's gold price.

On his way to Mecca, Mansa Musa gave gold to Cairo's officials, emirs and treasury, and his party spent freely. videos.title: Was the Rupee Ever Worth $1? 💵
videos.description:
Was 1 rupee equal to 1 dollar in 1947? The rupee vs dollar myth, fact-checked.
Rupee to dollar history: 1947, 1966, 1991 and today's near-record low.

In 1947 the rupee was pegged to the British pound, and a US dollar cost about ₹3.31 — never ₹1. India devalued to ₹7.50 per dollar in 1966, and after the 1991 balance-of-payments crisis the rate passed ₹30 within a year. In May 2026 the rupee hit a record low near ₹97; on 29 Oct 2026 it traded around ₹95. A weaker rupee also makes Indian exports cheaper abroad. Not financial advice.

videos.description:
Digital arrest scam explained: a "police officer" on a video call says you're under arrest — and the only way out is to move your money.
How the fake video-call arrest works, and the one rule that beats it.

One woman in India lost about ₹2.5 crore (~$260,000) in a single week. In 2024, Indians reported over 1.2 lakh digital-arrest cases and lost ₹1,918 crore (over $200 million). Police and agencies do not arrest anyone over a video call, and they never ask you to transfer money. On 29 Oct 2026 India's Supreme Court said banks that miss red flags should compensate victims. videos.title: Why Your $100 Ticket Costs $130 🎟️
videos.description:
Drip pricing shows a low price first and adds mandatory fees at checkout (the $100 to $130 ticket is an illustration). In a large StubHub field experiment (Blake, Moshary, Sweeney & Tadelis; Marketing Science, 2021), users who saw fees only at checkout spent about 21% more and were about 14% more likely to buy. The FTC's Rule on Unfair or Deceptive Fees, in effect since May 12, 2025, requires live-event ticket sellers and short-term lodging to show the total price, including mandatory fees, up front; taxes and shipping can still be added later. Tip: compare deals on the final checkout total.

videos.title: Tulip Mania 1637: The Bubble That Wasn't? 🌷
videos.description:
Legend says that at the peak of 1637's tulip mania, a single Semper Augustus bulb cost as much as an Amsterdam canal house; its reported price rose from about 1,200 guilders in the 1620s to an asked 10,000 guilders. Bulbs were traded on paper contracts while still in the ground, often in taverns, and in early February 1637 an auction in Haarlem drew no bids and prices collapsed within the week. But historian Anne Goldgar (Tulipmania, 2007) searched the records and could not find anyone who went bankrupt because of tulips; much of the famous drama comes from Charles Mackay's 1841 book. Economist Earl Thompson argued the peak prices reflected contract terms rather than a true bubble.

Scenes are drawn illustrations.

#Shorts #tulipmania #history

videos.title: Pay With a Gift Card? It's a Scam. Every Time 🎁
videos.description:
The FTC's rule of thumb: no real business or government agency will ever tell you to pay with a gift card. Scammers pose as the IRS, tech support or a utility about to cut your power, keep you on the phone while you buy cards (sometimes at several stores), then ask for the card number and PIN. With those, the money can be drained within minutes while you're still holding the card, and gift-card payments are hard to trace or reverse. Americans report losing over $200 million a year to gift-card payment scams (FTC Consumer Sentinel data). If someone demands one, hang up and report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

Scenes are drawn illustrations.

#Shorts #scamalert #giftcards

videos.title: Why Zimbabwe Printed a $100 Trillion Note 💵
videos.description:
Zimbabwe issued a 100-trillion-dollar note in January 2009; on its first day it was worth about US$30. In mid-November 2008 monthly inflation was estimated at 79.6 billion percent (Hanke & Kwok, Cato Journal), about 98% a day, with prices doubling roughly every 25 hours. The government removed 25 zeros in three redenominations (2006, 2008, 2009) before suspending the currency in April 2009 in favour of the US dollar and rand. In the 2015 demonetisation, accounts were converted at US$1 per 35 quadrillion Zimbabwe dollars, about 40 cents for a 100-trillion note. Today collectors pay around $100 for an uncirculated one, more than it was ever worth as money.

videos.title: Charles Ponzi Promised 50% in 45 Days 💸
videos.description:
In 1920 Charles Ponzi promised Boston investors 50% in 45 days, supposedly by buying international postal reply coupons cheaply abroad and redeeming them in the US. It couldn't work at scale, so he paid earlier investors with new investors' money. He took in roughly $15 million in about eight months (estimates range from about $10M to $15M; National Archives cites ~$15M). After the Boston Post's investigation, the scheme collapsed in August 1920; investor losses of about $20 million are over $200 million in today's dollars, and the Post won the 1921 Pulitzer Prize for Public Service. Ponzi served prison terms, was deported to Italy in 1934 and died in Rio de Janeiro in 1949.

Scenes are drawn illustrations.

#Shorts #PonziScheme #history

videos.title: The $6.50 Popcorn Trick Might Be a Myth 🍿
videos.description:
Why is the medium popcorn priced so close to the large? It may be a decoy: an option that exists to make another one look like a bargain. (The $3 / $6.50 / $7 prices are an illustration.)

The famous evidence is Dan Ariely's account of an Economist offer (web $59, print $125, print + web $125): he reported 84% of his MIT students picked the combo, and only 32% once the print-only option was removed. But that was a classroom exercise, not real subscribers; two of Ariely's other papers have since been retracted over data problems, and larger studies (Journal of Marketing Research, 2014) found the decoy effect weak or absent in many realistic settings. The useful test: would you buy the large without the medium?

Scenes are drawn illustrations.

#Shorts #pricing #psychology

videos.title: Why Prices End in .99 (It's Not the Cents) 🏷️
videos.description:
Why do prices end in .99? The left-digit effect: we read prices left to right and anchor on the first digit, so $9.99 feels like "nine-something" rather than ten.

It shows up in big purchases too: in more than 22 million wholesale used-car auction sales, prices dropped by roughly $150–$200 at each 10,000-mile odometer mark (Lacetera, Pope & Sydnor, NBER). And in a retail field experiment by Anderson (Chicago) and Simester (MIT), a dress sold better at $39 than at $34, suggesting a 9 ending itself signals a bargain. Tip: round up before you decide.

Scenes are drawn illustrations.

#Shorts #pricing #psychology

videos.title: Why Costco's Hot Dog Is Still $1.50 🌭
videos.description:
Costco's hot dog and soda combo has cost $1.50 since 1985. Adjusted for inflation it would be around $4.50 today, yet the price hasn't moved, and Costco sold more than 245 million combos in fiscal 2025.

It works as a loss leader: a deal so cheap it brings people in, and getting in takes a membership. In fiscal 2026 Costco earned about $5.9 billion in membership fees against roughly $9.2 billion of net income, so fees are about two-thirds the size of its profit. (The founder's "raise it and I'll kill you" line is the widely told story.)

Scenes are drawn illustrations.

#Shorts #Costco #pricing

videos.title: SEBI Barred 59 for This Stock-Tip Trap 📉
videos.description:
How a stock-tip "pump and dump" works: operators buy a small, cheap stock, a group fills with targets and profit screenshots, and once followers buy, the operators sell to them. The price falls, the group goes quiet, and victims get invited to a new one.

On 22 October 2026 SEBI cautioned investors about unregistered, invite-only WhatsApp groups that use planted members to fake profits. In a 2025 final order in a YouTube-driven pump-and-dump case (Sadhna Broadcast), SEBI barred 59 entities and ordered about ₹58 crore returned. Before trusting any tip, check the adviser's registration on SEBI's website. This is not investment advice. (The ₹500 target and profit screenshots shown are illustrative.)

videos.title: That 70% Off Was Never Real 🏷️
videos.description:
That "70% off" is only as real as the "was" price it's counted from. Before a sale, the crossed-out price can be pushed up, so ₹999 looks like a steal even if it sold for ₹999 all month.

India's amended e-commerce rules (notified September 2026, in force from 1 January 2027) require a discount to be shown next to the "prior price": the lowest price in the 30 days before the sale. EU rules already measure discounts this way, and in an EU check of 314 online traders around Black Friday and Cyber Monday, about 30% still displayed discounts incorrectly. Tip: check a product's price history before you trust the crossed-out number. (The ₹1,999 / ₹999 prices are an illustrative example.)

#Shorts #fakediscount #onlineshopping

videos.title: Milka Shrank 10%. Did You Notice? 🍫
videos.description:
Milka bars in Germany went from 100 g to 90 g in the same wrapper. That's shrinkflation: the price rise you don't see on the tag.

Why it works: in US store data (NielsenIQ, 2010–2020), a 1% price rise cut sales about 1.2%, but a 1% size cut hurt sales only about half as much. After a downsize, the price per unit rose about 12% on average. In 2016 Toblerone widened the gaps between its peaks, and in May 2026 a German court (Bremen) ruled the Milka cut misleading. The fix: compare the price per kilo, not the price tag.

Scenes are drawn illustrations.

#Shorts #shrinkflation #pricing

videos.title: Why Gold Fell 28% From Its Record?
videos.description:
Why is gold falling in 2026? Gold is down about 28% from its January record of $5,608, even with a war, $112 oil and hot inflation.
Gold pays no interest while a US government bond pays about 5%, and when stocks slide, people sell what they can. In moments like this, gold behaves less like a crisis shield and more like a bet that interest rates will fall.

videos.title: How AI Robots Are Helping The US Make More Honey | AI In Action
videos.description:
Sponsored by Quickbooks

Americans consume more than 600 million pounds of honey each year, so much that honey has to be imported to meet the demand. Honey depends on healthy bees, which are facing an uphill battle domestically, with about 50% of bee colonies dying in the US every year. Pests, like the Varroa mite, and environmental factors put hives at risk. 

So Nate's Honey and Sweet Harvest Foods are turning to artificial intelligence to help keep bees healthy. They use AI detection devices to monitor the sounds hives make. And they've employed a robotic hive that helps determine if mites are spreading. But can these technologies actually help the US make more honey?

videos.title: Why America Abandoned Route 66
videos.description:
In the 1940s and '50s, Route 66 was one of America's most popular highways, driving business to small towns from Chicago to Santa Monica. But today, the road and its people have been largely forgotten. Ghost towns, empty motels, and abandoned gas stations line its path. Chief correspondent Abby Narishkin grew up along the road. In celebration of its 100th anniversary, she drove down the old route herself to visit the people and businesses still keeping this Americana legacy alive.

videos.title: The $100 Billion Fashion Scam: How Shein Fooled the World
videos.description: How did Shein go from a nearly one-hundred-billion-dollar fast fashion empire to one of the most spectacular collapses the industry has ever witnessed? In this deep dive into the rise and fall of Shein, we trace the real story behind the eight-dollar dress, the invisible founder nobody can seem to find, and the search-engine trick that let a single man with a laptop outgrow Zara and H&M combined. We unpack the Shein business model piece by piece, the ultra fast fashion machine pumping out thousands of new styles a day, the questions swirling around its supply chain, and what actually happened when the company finally went public. Was it genius, or was it the biggest scam the fashion industry has ever pulled off? The numbers tell one story, but the method hidden behind the magic trick tells another. If you love business breakdowns on how fortunes are built and then vanish overnight, subscribe for more stories like this and hit the bell so you never miss the next one.

videos.title: From $605 Million To Nothing: How Juicy Couture Lost Everything
videos.description: The Juicy Couture rise and fall is one of the wildest stories in fashion, a velour tracksuit empire that went from two friends with 200 dollars to roughly 605 million dollars in sales, then watched its American stores go dark. In this business documentary we trace the Juicy Couture history from cut-up maternity jeans in Los Angeles to Madonna, Paris Hilton and Britney Spears making the Juicy Couture tracksuit the uniform of 2000s Y2K fashion. Then the money men arrived. You will see what Liz Claiborne really paid for the brand, the strange secret behind its Fifth Avenue flagship, why the founders walked away, and how a landlord ended up paying Juicy to leave. If you have ever wondered what happened to Juicy Couture, and who is really to blame for the Juicy Couture rise and fall, this is the full story most people never heard. Subscribe for more deep dives into the brands you grew up with, and tell us in the comments whether you owned a Juicy tracksuit.

videos.title: Birkenstock: How To Make BILLIONS From Ugly Shoes 🤮💸
videos.description: How did the ugliest shoe in the world turn into a brand worth more than eight and a half billion dollars? This is the incredible Birkenstock story, the rise of a flat, lumpy, foot-shaped sandal that buyers literally laughed out of the room in 1963, and the two-hundred-and-fifty-year family obsession that refused to let it die. We go all the way back to a village cobbler in 1774, to the inventor who asked why shoes are built flat when the human foot is not, and forward to the day that same "hippie footwear" rang the bell at the New York Stock Exchange. Along the way we unpack how Birkenstock became a luxury fashion phenomenon, the business decisions that turned mockery into obsession, and the surprising names that ended up betting billions on an orthopedic sandal. How exactly do you make billions from ugly shoes? The answer is stranger and smarter than you would ever guess. If you love brand origin stories and business breakdowns, subscribe for more stories like this and hit the bell so you never miss one.

videos.title: Why The Founder of Jimmy Choo Left Jimmy Choo
videos.description: Why did the founder of Jimmy Choo leave Jimmy Choo? His shoes walked the red carpet at the Oscars, Princess Diana wore them, and the brand grew into a global empire worth over a billion dollars. Yet the quiet shoemaker from Penang whose name is on every pair walked away. This is the real Jimmy Choo founder story, from a boy stitching his first slipper at eleven to a workshop in East London that caught the eye of British Vogue. You'll meet Tamara Mellon, the fashion insider who helped turn his craft into a business, and Tom Yeardye, the investor who backed the deal. You'll also hear about Sandra Choi, Lion Capital and the buyers who came later, and why the name on the label no longer belongs to the man who earned it. If you love rags-to-riches stories and the ugly side of luxury, this one is for you. Subscribe for more true brand stories and tell us in the comments who really deserves credit.
tags: why the founder of Jimmy Choo left

videos.title: $625 Million To Forgotten: How TOMS Lost Everything
videos.description: How did TOMS Shoes go from a six-hundred-and-twenty-five-million-dollar valuation to handing the keys to its creditors in just five years? This is the full rise and fall of TOMS, the story of a restless Texas entrepreneur named Blake Mycoskie who turned a dusty road in Argentina into one of the most famous shoe companies on Earth, built entirely on a single radical idea. We break down how the One for One model made TOMS a cultural phenomenon, why the giving strategy that built everything may have quietly been the thing that broke it, and what really happened when private equity came knocking. Was it a feel-good business ahead of its time, or a model that was never built to last? The founder who once called himself Chief Shoe Giver ended up with none of it, and the reason why is more complicated than anyone expected. If you love business breakdowns on how companies rise fast and lose it all, subscribe for more stories like this and turn on notifications so you never miss one.

videos.title: Lululemon Is Losing Everything: Leggings, Shoppers & Shareholders on the Brink
videos.description: Why is Lululemon losing everything? In December 2023 the yoga pants company hit a record $511 a share and was worth more than Ford and General Motors, with analysts calling it unstoppable. Now the stock has crashed, rivals are stealing its customers, and even its own founder is picking a fight. This is the Lululemon decline explained, from the brand that turned leggings into a status symbol to the cracks that started showing behind the scenes. You'll meet Chip Wilson, hear how Alo Yoga became the new favorite of celebrities like Kendall Jenner, Hailey Bieber and Bella Hadid, and find out why a famous Big Short investor started circling the stock. We look at what Lululemon got right, what it got wrong, and the question nobody on Wall Street wants to answer. If you love business documentaries about big brands in trouble, you'll want to see the whole story. Subscribe for more deep dives into how empires rise and fall, and tell us in the comments if you still wear Lululemon.

videos.title: $700 Million To Forgotten: How Ed Hardy Lost Everything
videos.description: What happened to Ed Hardy? At its peak in 2009, one tattoo artist's tiger was on T-shirts, trucker hats, perfume, energy drinks and even toothbrushes, and the Ed Hardy name was tied to more than $700 million in sales. Two years later, the rights sold for a fraction of that, nightclubs were banning the shirts, and the man whose name was on every label could barely stand to look at it. This is the rise and fall of Ed Hardy, from a respected San Francisco tattoo master to a Y2K punchline. You'll meet the flashy French designer behind the empire, the $100 million lawsuit, a reality TV divorce, and a certain MTV show that changed everything. And the ending, with the museum retrospective and the Gen Z comeback, might surprise you. If you remember the rhinestone shirts or love brand collapse documentaries, this one is for you. Subscribe for more deep dives into how famous brands were built and lost, and tell us in the comments if you ever owned an Ed Hardy shirt.
tags: rise and fall of Ed Hardy

videos.title: How A Poor Japanese Soldier Created ASICS
videos.description: How did a former Japanese army officer with no trade, no money and not even his birth name end up building ASICS? This is the ASICS founder story of Kihachiro Onitsuka, who came home from World War Two to a bombed-out Kobe carrying nothing but a promise to a friend who never returned. From a two-person shoe workshop to one of the biggest sportswear companies in the world, the Onitsuka Tiger history is full of strange turns: an octopus on a dinner plate, a barefoot Olympic champion, and a young American who showed up with a company that didn't exist yet. You'll find out how that partnership started, why it turned into one of the most famous breakups in business, and where the name ASICS really comes from. Plus the surprising comeback that has the brand posting record numbers today. If you love founder origin stories, sneaker history, or the story behind Nike's rival, this one is for you. Subscribe for more true stories behind the world's biggest brands, and tell us your favorite pair of ASICS in the comments.

videos.title: From $2.4 Billion To Nothing: How Aéropostale Lost Everything
videos.description: What happened to Aéropostale? In 2010 the teen mall giant pulled in $2.4 billion in sales and its logo hoodie was in nearly every high school hallway in America. Six years later it was in bankruptcy court, accusing its own biggest backer of sinking it. This is the rise and fall of Aéropostale, from a forgotten Macy's private label to a Wall Street darling, and the strange chain of events that followed. You'll meet the executive who bought 119 stores and turned them into a teen empire, a private equity rescue deal with strings nobody noticed, and a courtroom fight over who really killed the brand. And the ending, with mall landlords, fast fashion and a famous retail name still in the mix, is one most people never saw coming. If you grew up shopping in the mall, or love retail bankruptcy documentaries, you'll want to see how a $2.4 billion brand lost it all. Subscribe for more true stories of brands that rose and fell, and leave a comment with your favorite Aéropostale memory.

videos.title: From $1.7 Billion To Nothing: How Yeezy Lost Everything
videos.description: In 2020, Yeezy did nearly $1.7 billion in sales and turned Kanye West into a billionaire Forbes valued at $6.6 billion — and then it all vanished. This is how Yeezy lost everything: the Kanye West and Adidas deal that beat the royalties Nike refused him, the Red October saga that started it all, the scarcity machine behind every Yeezy Boost 350 drop, and the single overlooked clause in the Adidas Kanye contract that decided who would survive the collapse. We trace the rise and fall of Yeezy from a $53 million debt tweet and a billion-dollar ask that never came, to the Yeezy Gap ten-year deal, to the October 2022 press release that erased a sneaker empire overnight. Why could Adidas walk away intact while Kanye's net worth cratered? What did he actually own — and what did he only rent? The answer is hiding in plain sight, and it changes how you see the whole empire. Watch to the end to see exactly how the money moved, and who was left holding nothing. If you love deep-dive business stories like this, subscribe for more rise-and-fall breakdowns every week.
tags: how Adidas made Kanye a billionaire

videos.title: How A Poor Boy Created Benetton
videos.description: This is the Benetton founder story that sounds too wild to be true: a ten-year-old boy from Treviso loses his father, quits school at fourteen, and sells his bicycle just to buy a single knitting machine. That decision, made with his sister Giuliana, would eventually turn into one of Italy's most recognizable fashion empires, and this Luciano Benetton biography traces every twist of the Benetton founder story along the way. You'll see how four siblings built a piece of United Colors of Benetton history from a spare room into a global franchise network, and how photographer Oliviero Toscani's controversial ads turned a sweater company into a lightning rod for scandal, censorship, and headlines around the world. What really happened behind the boldest campaigns anyone dared print? How did a family business survive a Benetton rise and fall that few brands ever recover from? And what does the Benetton family fashion empire look like heading into 2026? Stick around, because the answers are stranger than the sweaters. If you love rags-to-riches business stories, underdog founders, and the real history behind the brands you grew up wearing, subscribe for more stories like this — new documentaries drop regularly.
tags: how a poor boy created Benetton

videos.title: How An Immigrant Seamstress Created Maidenform
videos.description: The story of Ida Rosenthal and Maidenform begins not in a boardroom but on a ship out of the Russian Empire, where a young Jewish seamstress from Rakov, Belarus arrived in America with almost nothing but a needle, thread, and an idea nobody else in the garment industry had thought to try. What started as a small alteration shop in New York would eventually reshape how the entire world thinks about women's undergarments, but getting there meant Ida had to solve a problem the biggest names in fashion had ignored for decades, and the breakthrough she landed on would quietly become an industry standard still used today. Along the way there were setbacks, a stubborn husband-turned-business-partner, fierce competitors who doubted a foreign-born woman could build anything lasting, and a single design decision that changed everything. This is the real, largely untold history of how one immigrant's grit and eye for detail turned a struggling sewing shop into a household name recognized in nearly every American home. Curious how far a needle and thread can really take you? Watch the full story to find out exactly how it happened, and subscribe for more stories like this.
tags: how bra cup sizes were invented

videos.title: How A Cigar Roller's Son Created Revlon
videos.description: He was the son of a cigar roller with no chemistry degree, no money, and no plan B, yet Charles Revson would turn a $300 investment into Revlon, one of the biggest cosmetics empires in history. This is the real Charles Revson Revlon founder story: how a rejected nail polish salesman built an opaque cream enamel formula in the middle of the Great Depression, fought dirty against rivals like Charles of the Ritz, and went head-to-head with Estee Lauder for control of America's beauty counters. You'll see how Revlon's marketing genius, from the daring Fire and Ice campaign to its infamous sponsorship of a rigged 1950s game show, nearly unraveled everything he built, and how he walked away from a congressional scandal with his empire bigger than ever. This is the untold Revlon company history behind the lipstick, the perfume, and the ruthless perfectionist who built it all from nothing. If you love rags-to-riches business documentaries about the real people behind America's biggest brands, subscribe for more incredible true stories like this one.

videos.title: How A Dressmaker's Son Created Bill Blass
videos.description: Bill Blass fashion designer isn't just a name on a label -- it's the story of a boy from Fort Wayne, Indiana, who turned early tragedy and hardship into one of the great careers in American fashion history. Raised largely by his mother, a dressmaker who held the family together through the Depression, young Bill grew up watching a needle and thread do what words couldn't. This is the untold Bill Blass biography behind the sketches, the sewing machine, and the relentless drive that carried him from a small Midwestern bedroom to New York's garment district. Along the way there's a wartime twist most fashion history documentary fans have never heard, a scrappy climb through an industry that didn't want to make room for him, and a showdown on a Paris stage in 1973 -- the legendary Battle of Versailles fashion show -- that changed American fashion icon status forever. How does a kid who lost so much as a child end up dressing First Ladies and Hollywood royalty? What really happened backstage in Versailles? Watch to find out how a dressmaker's son rewrote the rules of American elegance -- and subscribe for more stories like this.

videos.title: From $300 Million to Nothing: How Airwalk Lost Everything
videos.description: The rise and fall of Airwalk is one of the wildest brand collapse stories of the 90s: a skate shoe company that went from near-bankruptcy to roughly 300 million dollars a year, then vanished almost overnight. In this business documentary we trace the full Airwalk shoes history, from a private-label factory in Pennsylvania to the feet of Tony Hawk and half the teenagers in America, back when the pterodactyl logo sat on the same cool list as Pepsi and Levi's. So what happened to Airwalk? How did one of the most influential skate shoe brands on the planet end up on the clearance racks at Payless for twenty dollars a pair? We dig into the marketing genius that built it, the single decision that quietly destroyed it, and the reason core skaters walked away without a goodbye. If you love stories about famous brands that disappeared, skate culture, and the business mistakes that sink empires, this one will stick with you. Subscribe for more rise and fall stories like this every week, and drop a comment with the next brand you want us to break down.

videos.title: From $136 Million to Nothing: How British Knights Lost Everything
videos.description: British Knights sneakers were once one of the hottest shoe brands in America, jumping from $8 million to $136 million in sales in just three years, so how did the famous BK button end up in the bargain bin? This business documentary traces the rise and fall of British Knights, from a quiet Tribeca dress shoe company founded in 1936 to the loud 80s sneaker brand that put Kool Moe Dee and MC Hammer in its commercials and took open shots at Nike. Along the way you'll hear about the Blood Killer rumor that got BKs banned from schools, a gold chain shoe that sparked outrage, a contest built on smelly socks, and one surprising admission from inside the family business. If you've ever wondered what happened to British Knights, or why so many forgotten 90s sneaker brands vanished while Nike kept growing, this story has twists you won't see coming. The British Knights sneakers you remember from Foot Locker had a far stranger journey than most people realize. Subscribe for more untold stories behind the brands you grew up with, and tell us in the comments whether you owned a pair of BKs.

videos.title: From $818 Million to Nothing: How L.A. Gear Lost Everything
videos.description: LA Gear looked unstoppable — for a few dazzling years, this scrappy California sneaker company outsold nearly everyone in America except Nike and Reebok, turning a Melrose Avenue storefront into a billion-dollar Wall Street darling. You'll discover the gutsy decision that changed everything, the secret ingredient that set Hershey's apart from every European chocolatier, and the jaw-dropping reason Milton gave away his entire fortune before he died. videos.title: The Brothers Behind Adidas & Puma Had a Dark Secret
videos.description:
Adidas and Puma are two of the biggest sportswear brands in the world.

But few people know that they were created by two brothers who once ran the same family shoe company.

Adolf “Adi” Dassler and Rudolf Dassler started making shoes together in Herzogenaurach, Germany. Their business grew rapidly, their shoes reached elite athletes, and Jesse Owens famously wore Dassler spikes during the 1936 Berlin Olympics.

But as Nazi Germany rose, the brothers became increasingly entangled in the political and economic system of the era. Both joined the Nazi Party in 1933, and their company later became involved in wartime production.

After World War II, the brothers' relationship completely collapsed.

In 1948, Rudolf Dassler left the family business and founded what would become Puma. Adi remained behind and founded Adidas in 1949.

What followed was one of the most extraordinary rivalries in business history.

Adidas and Puma became fierce competitors. Their rivalry divided the small German town of Herzogenaurach, influenced professional athletes, and eventually reached some of the biggest names in sports—including Pelé.

This is the story of the Dassler brothers, the family feud behind Adidas and Puma, and how one broken relationship created two global sportswear empires.

videos.title: Kodak Invented the Digital Camera So Why Did It Fall?  #KodakHistory #DigitalCamera #Failure #Shorts
videos.description:
Kodak helped millions of people capture their most important memories. For decades, it was one of the biggest names in photography.

But here's the surprising part: Kodak engineer Steven Sasson developed an early digital camera prototype in 1975. Even with this technological breakthrough, Kodak struggled as digital photography transformed the industry.

In this short documentary, discover Kodak's rise, its connection to the early digital camera, and the challenges that eventually led the company to file for bankruptcy protection in 2012.

videos.description:
What Happened to Crazy Eddie? The TV Pitchman Who Stole $75 Million

"His prices are INSAAAANE!" was the most recognizable commercial in 1980s New York. It was also, in a way nobody watching could have guessed, the biggest lie on television.

Crazy Eddie Antar built a chain of electronics stores in Brooklyn in 1969 into a tri-state retail phenomenon, fueled by genuinely low prices and a manic TV pitchman played by Jerry Carroll. But from its earliest days, the Antar family was running a cash-skimming operation, hiding tens of millions of dollars in revenue from the IRS. When Eddie Antar decided to take the company public in 1984, the family reversed the fraud entirely — smuggling the hidden cash back into the country and recording it as phantom inventory to inflate the company's profits ahead of the IPO. Crazy Eddie raised roughly $74 million going public, and family members sold tens of millions more in stock over the following years. After a hostile takeover in 1987, new management ordered a physical inventory count and discovered approximately $45 million in inventory simply did not exist. Eddie Antar fled to Israel on a false passport in 1990, was tracked down by the FBI and Interpol, extradited in 1992, and ultimately served over six years in federal prison. The SEC and civil litigants recovered more than $75 million from Antar and his associates.

videos.title: What Happened to Sam Goody? The Music Empire Killed by a College Kid's Software

Best Buy Bought Musicland for $685 Million — Then Sold It for $0

In 2001, Best Buy paid $685 million for Musicland, the parent company of mall mainstay Sam Goody, betting on the booming CD market at its all-time peak. Weeks later, Napster went mainstream. Two and a half years later, Best Buy gave the entire company away for nothing.

Musicland's roughly 1,500 Sam Goody, Suncoast, and Media Play stores were, for decades, the cultural center of the American mall — the place where a generation of teenagers discovered music at the listening station wall before spending their allowance on a CD. By 2000, Musicland was a billion-dollar business at the exact peak of global CD sales. Best Buy saw an opportunity to convert those mall locations into outposts for electronics and MP3 players. Instead, the acquisition collided with the fastest format collapse in retail history: Napster's free downloads, home CD burners, and then Apple's iTunes store gutted the entire reason to walk into a music store. In June 2003, Best Buy sold Musicland to private equity firm Sun Capital Partners, which assumed roughly $500 million in liabilities and paid no cash at all. Best Buy took a $66 million after-tax loss on the deal. Sun Capital spent the following years closing stores and liquidating chains, including Media Play in 2006, and what remained of Musicland filed for bankruptcy that same year.

videos.title: What Happened to Lehman Brothers? The 158-Year-Old Bank That Died in a Weekend
videos.description:
What Happened to Lehman Brothers? The 158-Year-Old Bank That Died in a Weekend

Lehman Brothers survived the Civil War, the Panic of 1907, the Great Depression, two world wars, and the savings and loan crisis. In September 2008, it didn't survive one weekend of closed-door meetings at the Federal Reserve.

Founded in 1850 as a dry goods and cotton trading shop in Montgomery, Alabama, Lehman Brothers grew into one of the five largest investment banks on Wall Street. Under CEO Richard Fuld, the firm pushed aggressively into mortgage-backed securities through the 2000s, acquiring five mortgage lenders outright and pushing its leverage past 30 to 1. When housing prices collapsed starting in 2006, Lehman's real estate exposure became catastrophic — and a court-appointed examiner later found the firm used an accounting maneuver internally called "Repo 105" to move up to $50 billion off its balance sheet at the end of each quarter, temporarily hiding the true scale of its debt from investors and regulators.

By September 2008, with talks for a capital injection from Korea Development Bank collapsed and no buyer willing to move without government backing, Lehman Brothers had nowhere left to turn. In the early hours of September 15, 2008, the firm filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy with $639 billion in assets — still the largest bankruptcy filing in American history. videos.title: What Happened to TWA? The Billionaire's Airline That Ended in a Ball of Fire
videos.description:
TWA didn't just fade away like most dead airlines. It was destroyed twice — once by a Wall Street corporate raider who gutted it for parts, and once by a catastrophic explosion that traced directly back to the damage he left behind.

Trans World Airlines was built by eccentric billionaire Howard Hughes into the most glamorous airline on Earth — the first to premiere in-flight movies and color TV, the airline of Hollywood royalty, home to the iconic Eero Saarinen-designed terminal at JFK. Then in 1985, corporate raider Carl Icahn seized control of TWA, completing a hostile leveraged buyout by 1988. He sold off the airline's assets to repay the debt used to acquire it — a strategy that earned him the label "corporate raider" and made TWA a textbook case of asset stripping. In 1991, he sold TWA's most valuable asset, its London Heathrow landing slots, to American Airlines for $445 million — pocketing an estimated $469 million personal profit while leaving TWA saddled with $540 million in debt.

Five years later, on July 17, 1996, TWA Flight 800 exploded over the Atlantic Ocean off Long Island, killing all 230 people on board. Over 200 eyewitnesses reported seeing a streak of light, and the FBI launched a parallel criminal investigation amid fears of terrorism. videos.title: The Real Reason Toys R Us Died (It Wasn't Amazon)
videos.description:
Toys R Us wasn't killed by Amazon. It wasn't killed by iPads or changing kids' habits. It was killed by Wall Street.

In 2005, private equity firms Bain Capital, KKR, and Vornado Realty Trust bought Toys R Us in a $6.6 billion leveraged buyout — and loaded $5.3 billion of debt directly onto the company they had just purchased. For the next 12 years, Toys R Us paid over $5 billion in interest just to survive, while its private equity owners collected $470 million in fees. In September 2017, the company filed for bankruptcy. By March 2018, all 735 U.S. stores were gone, and 33,000 workers lost their jobs with zero severance pay.

This is the full story of how a private equity leveraged buyout destroyed one of the most iconic retail chains in American history — and how the workers who lost everything fought back.

videos.title: The Eighth Crusade (1270) | The King Who Never Reached Jerusalem | Medieval History
videos.description:
This video tells the story of the Eighth Crusade, the final crusading expedition of Louis IX, a campaign that never came close to reaching Jerusalem.

After the setbacks of the Seventh Crusade, Louis remained committed to the crusading cause and spent years preparing a new expedition. In 1270, he led an army across the Mediterranean, but instead of sailing directly to the Holy Land, the crusaders targeted the North African city of Tunis.

The reasons for this decision have long been debated by historians. Some believed Tunis could become an ally or provide a strategic base for future operations against Muslim powers in the eastern Mediterranean. Whatever the plan, the campaign quickly ran into difficulties.

Disease spread through the crusader camp during the hot summer months, weakening the army before any major achievements could be secured. Among those who fell ill was Louis IX himself. The French king died near Tunis before his crusade could advance any further, bringing the expedition's momentum to an abrupt end.

This gentle bedtime history explores the Eighth Crusade as a story of determination, changing strategies, and the final journey of one of the most famous crusading kings—told in a calm and reflective way to help you rest.

videos.description:

videos.title: The Rise and Fall of WeWork: How a $47 Billion Empire Collapsed in Six Weeks
videos.description:
It rented desks. That is all it ever really did. Yet at its peak, WeWork was valued at $47 billion — worth more than Ford, more than General Motors — and its founder promised to "elevate the world's consciousness." This is the story of the most spectacular illusion in modern business history.

In 2010, Adam Neumann and Miguel McKelvey opened a single shared office in New York. What followed was a rocket ride fuelled by other people's money: SoftBank poured in billions, and Masayoshi Son — after a twelve-minute meeting — told Neumann he wasn't crazy enough, that in a fight, "the crazy man wins." WeWork invented its own accounting, reporting a metric called "community-adjusted EBITDA" that simply erased its costs. In 2018 it lost $1.9 billion on $1.8 billion of revenue — and its valuation kept climbing.

Then came the IPO filing. The S-1 exposed everything: Neumann had personally trademarked the word "We" and sold it back to his own company for $5.9 million; he had cashed out more than $700 million before the IPO while the company burned cash; the prospectus opened with a dedication "to the energy of we." Investors revolted. In six weeks the $47 billion empire collapsed to the edge of bankruptcy. Neumann walked away with a $1.7 billion exit package while 2,400 employees lost their jobs. Son later admitted publicly: "It was foolish of me to invest in WeWork."

WeWork eventually went public through a SPAC, then filed for Chapter 11 in 2023. And Adam Neumann? He raised $350 millio

videos.title: The story of kodak" See kodak's rise & fall in full video.What you will learn from it?
videos.description:
In 1975, inside a Kodak laboratory in Rochester, New York, a 24-year-old engineer named Steven Sasson built the world's first digital camera. It was heavy, it was slow — and it was the future. Kodak's executives looked at it and reportedly said: "That's cute — but don't tell anyone."

At the time, Kodak controlled ninety percent of America's film market. Film was a money-printing machine, and digital threatened every cent of it. So Kodak patented its own invention — and locked it in a drawer.

Kodak even saw the cliff coming. Its own 1981 study predicted digital photography would take over, and gave the company roughly ten years to prepare. Ten years of warning, delivered by its own analysts — and still, when the digital wave broke, Kodak clung to film while the future it invented was sold to everyone else.

In January 2012, the company that taught the world to capture its memories filed for bankruptcy. Its digital imaging patents — the very technology Sasson had pioneered — were sold off to the technology giants that had eaten its future.

This is the full story: George Eastman's wooden box camera, the "Kodak moment," the invention buried to protect a monopoly, the ten-year warning nobody acted on, and the slowest-motion collapse in business history.

videos.title: The COMPLETE History of the Romanian Securitate in 11 Minutes
videos.description:
On August 30, 1948, Romania’s new communist rulers created a secret police force that would terrorize the country for more than four decades. The Securitate began as a tool built with Soviet help to crush opposition, and it grew into one of the most feared intelligence and surveillance agencies in the Eastern Bloc. In this complete documentary on the history of the Romanian Securitate, we trace the story from the Soviet-backed communist takeover after World War II to the brutal political prisons of Sighet and Pitești, the labor camps of the Danube–Black Sea Canal, and the hunt for anti-communist resistance fighters in the Carpathian Mountains. We then follow the rise of Nicolae Ceaușescu, his dramatic 1968 speech against the invasion of Czechoslovakia, and the mass surveillance state that followed, built on telephone tapping, censorship, and a vast network of informants. Finally, we reach the 1989 Romanian Revolution, the fall and execution of the Ceaușescus, and the unanswered questions that still surround the Securitate today. This is the dark history of communist Romania, the secret police behind the Iron Curtain, and the legacy that Romanians are still confronting.

🕵️ Understand how a secret police force controlled an entire nation

videos.title: André Marie Ampère: The Birth of Electrodynamics
videos.description:
What happens when pure mathematical precision meets unimaginable personal tragedy?

When the scientific world first saw a compass needle twitch near a live electric wire, most dismissed it as a curious anomaly. But André-Marie Ampère recognized something far greater—a fundamental mechanical force of nature.

In this episode of Chronicle Note, explore the life and mind of André-Marie Ampère. Driven by personal loss during the French Revolution, Ampère sought refuge in absolute mathematical order. In a single relentless sprint of laboratory trials and derivations, he removed magnetic iron from the equation, proved that moving electric charges exert direct forces on each other, invented the solenoid, and laid the foundations of electrodynamics.
From the basic physics of wire attraction and repulsion to the superconducting solenoids powering hospital MRI scanners and modern electric vehicle motors, discover how one scholar's breakthroughs became the physical engine of modern civilization.

In this video, you'll discover:
* How Ampère proved electric currents act directly on each other
* The intuitive physics behind parallel currents, water stream analogies, and wire forces
* The genius of the solenoid and the stadium-stunt model of microscopic molecular currents
* How a quiet scholar's formulas paved the way for modern electric transport and medical technology

🔔 Subscribe to Chronicle Note for deep-dive historical documentaries on the visionaries, breakthroughs, and hidden stori

videos.title: Hans Christian Ørsted and the Discovery of Electromagnetism
videos.description:
For generations, natural philosophers believed electricity and magnetism were two completely separate forces governing the cosmos. That consensus shattered in a single Copenhagen lecture hall when Hans Christian Ørsted brought a live battery wire near a compass needle and watched it turn perpendicular.

In this episode of Chronicle Note, we uncover the high-stakes story of an apothecary’s son who defied Europe’s scientific elite to prove that electricity and magnetism share a single universal harmony. From his humble roots in Rudkøbing to isolating metallic aluminum and pioneering thought experiments, discover the human drama, bitter rivalries, and primary source truths behind the pioneer who lit the spark driving our modern electric civilization.

videos.title: The Crooked E: The Rise and Fall of Enron | From Gas Pipelines to America's Biggest Bankruptcy
videos.description:
Sunday, December 2nd, 2001. In a federal bankruptcy court in Manhattan, a Houston company listing $63.4 billion in assets files for Chapter 11. At that moment, it is the largest corporate bankruptcy in American history. Its name is Enron.

Enron didn't begin as a trading floor. It began as natural gas pipelines laid across Texas and the Great Plains: Houston Natural Gas in 1925 and Northern Natural Gas in Omaha in 1930. In 1985 they merged, and under Ken Lay, a preacher's son with a doctorate in economics, the new company grew into "America's Most Innovative Company" six years in a row.

In this documentary: the name that almost was, the Valhalla warning, Skilling's Gas Bank, the 1992 mark-to-market letter, Teesside and Dabhol, the crooked E and "Ask Why", rank and yank, Fastow's partnerships and the Raptors, Enron Field, EnronOnline, the California crisis, Sherron Watkins's memo, the 401(k) freeze, $90.75 to 61 cents, Arthur Andersen, the courtroom years, and the old pipeline that still runs today.

So who brought down Enron? Deregulation, mark-to-market, the culture, the partnerships, or the people whose job was to ask why?

I'm Grace. I studied economics in the U.S. Pour a coffee, settle in, and join me for the last shift.

This video is history and education, not financial advice.

videos.title: Same Year as Walmart, Way Out in Front | The Rise and Fall of Kmart
videos.description:
Tuesday, January 22nd, 2002. In Chicago, a company with seventeen billion dollars in assets files for Chapter 11. It is the biggest retail bankruptcy in American history at the time. Its name is Kmart.

Kmart began as S.S. Kresge's dime stores, built out of pennies by a tinware salesman born in 1867. In 1962, the first full-size Kmart opened in Garden City, Michigan, the same year Target and Walmart opened their first stores. Kmart was way out in front. It gave America the Blue Light Special, layaway, Jaclyn Smith and Martha Stewart, and at its peak about 2,486 stores.

In this documentary, we follow Harry Cunningham's $80 million bet, a police light in Fort Wayne, the shopping spree of Waldenbooks, Borders, OfficeMax and The Sports Authority, the half-billion-dollar gap with Walmart in 1990, the light that went dark in 1991, BlueLight Always, the 2002 bankruptcy, the 2005 deal that made Kmart buy Sears, and the last full-size store on the mainland in Bridgehampton, New York.

So who took down Kmart? Walmart, the price war, the spending spree, or the company itself?

videos.title: They Sold the One Part That Survived | The Rise and Fall of Tower Records
videos.description:
Friday, December 22, 2006. After forty-six years, the last Tower Records stores in America lock their doors. Seven years earlier, the company sold more than a billion dollars of music a year. On a marquee in Sacramento, four words go up: All Things Must Pass.

Tower Records began with a teenager selling used jukebox records for ten cents in his father's drugstore, inside a movie theater called the Tower. It became the most famous record store in the world: open until midnight on the Sunset Strip, a four-story landmark on Broadway, a giant flagship on Piccadilly Circus, and nine floors of music in Shibuya. Elton John said he probably spent more money there than any other human being.

In this documentary, we follow Russ Solomon from a three-cent jukebox record to a $5,000 loan from his dad, 8801 Sunset Boulevard, the clerks hired for what they knew, Tokyo and No Music, No Life, the junk bonds of 1998, Napster, the $16.99 CD against $9.99 loss leaders, the sale of Tower Records Japan, iTunes, two bankruptcies, the $134.3 million auction that a liquidator won by half a million dollars, and the last night on Sunset.

So who killed Tower Records? The internet, the discount giants, debt, or the album itself?

I'm Grace. I studied economics in the U.S. Pour a coffee, settle in, and join me for the last shift.

videos.title: They Invented the Instant Photo. Then Your Phone Took It. | The Fall of Polaroid
videos.description:
October 11, 2001. One month after September 11th, late in the day in Delaware, the company that taught the world to watch a picture appear in its hand files for bankruptcy. It owes close to a billion dollars. Seven years later, in a small Dutch city called Enschede, the last factory making its film is about to shut down for good.

For fifty years, Polaroid was one of the most exciting companies on Earth. A three-year-old's question in Santa Fe became the first instant camera. It made the SX-70, helped build the U-2 spy plane, put cameras in the hands of Andy Warhol and Ansel Adams, and beat Kodak in court. Then it went bankrupt. Twice.

In this documentary, we follow Edwin Land from a cheap plastic polarizer to a walk in Santa Fe in 1943, the SX-70, the workers who protested apartheid, Polavision, the nearly $1 billion win against Kodak, the digital camera Polaroid saw coming, October 11, 2001, and the ten workers in Enschede who saved the film.

So who killed Polaroid? Digital, the razor-and-blades model, debt and management, or the genius himself?

videos.description:
December 4, 1991. A Boeing 727 named Clipper Goodwill comes in low over Miami, on its way home from Barbados. Hundreds of airline workers are standing on the ramp, watching. That morning, the company that owned this plane stopped flying. This was the last Pan Am flight that would ever carry paying passengers.

For forty years, Pan Am wasn't just an airline. It was the airline. It flew the first airmail across the Pacific, the first regular airplane passenger flights across the Atlantic, America's first jets across the ocean, and the world's first 747. It had its own skyscraper on top of Grand Central, its own luxury hotels, and a waiting list of more than 90,000 people for a flight to the Moon.

In this documentary, we go back to a borrowed floatplane and seven bags of mail in Key West in 1927. We follow Juan Trippe and his globe, the Clipper flying boats, the islands Pan Am built in the middle of the Pacific, the Pacific Clipper's long way home in 1941, tourist class, the jet age, the Worldport and the Pan Am Building, the stewardesses, and the First Moon Flights Club. Then the long fall: too many seats, deregulation, the National merger, selling the crown jewels, Tenerife, Flight 73, Lockerbie, and December 4, 1991.

So who grounded Pan Am? The government, bad luck, the managers who came after Trippe, or the dream itself?

videos.description:
Kansas, winter of 1908. On the kitchen table of a farmhouse thirty miles from town sits a thousand-page book, and everything in it can arrive at the door: a watch, a bicycle, a violin, even a whole house. That book was the Sears, Roebuck catalog. The company behind it became the biggest retailer on Earth and built the tallest building in the world. By the summer of 2026, only five full Sears department stores were left in the mainland United States.

In this documentary, we go back to a railroad station in North Redwood, Minnesota, and a box of pocket watches nobody wanted. We follow Richard Sears and Alvah Roebuck, Julius Rosenwald's money-back promise and the Rosenwald Schools, the giant Chicago mail-order plant, Parcel Post, houses sold by mail in boxcars, General Robert E. Wood's bet on stores, Craftsman, Kenmore, Allstate and the Wish Book. Then the long fall: the Sears Tower, socks and stocks, Walmart, January 25, 1993, the Kmart merger, selling the family silver, and October 15, 2018.

So who killed Sears? Walmart and Amazon, a hedge fund manager, earlier management, or something nobody likes to name?

November 18, 1995. A steel mill on the south bank of the Lehigh River in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania. A crowd of men in hard hats watches a blast furnace tapped for the very last time. Then we follow the long fall: the 116-day strike of 1959, the wrong furnace, Black Friday in 1977, Lackawanna and Johnstown, the pension promises that came due, and October 15, 2001.

So who killed Bethlehem Steel? Foreign competition, the union, management, or something nobody likes to name?

February 2026. A brick factory on Myrtle Street in New Britain, Connecticut. A few hundred people making the yellow tape measures that are probably sitting in your kitchen drawer right now find out the plant is closing. About 300 jobs. And Stanley had been making things in this city since 1843.

In this documentary, we go back to Frederick Stanley's little steam-powered bolt shop, the two rival Stanley companies, the Bailey hand plane that ended up on carpenters' benches around the world, and two young men in Baltimore who sold a car to start Black & Decker and put a pistol-grip drill in everyone's hands, and even sent one to the Moon with Apollo. Then we follow the long retreat: the Bermuda tax fight, the China shock, the 2010 merger that created Stanley Black & Decker, the Craftsman promise, and the pandemic boom and bust.

The company never went bankrupt. So how does the beating heart of the Hardware City become a headquarters with no factory floor?

videos.title: The Horrors of Devil's Island
videos.description:
A wooden wall built so close to a prison hut that it blocked out the daylight, with one purpose: to hide the sea from the man inside. That man was Alfred Dreyfus, and his cell was only one corner of a vast penal colony that France ran in Guiana under the law. This is the story of the Îles du Salut: how a sentence could mean never going home, how many men really died and why nobody can give a clean number, the famous book that historians say was partly borrowed, the reporter who exposed it, and the islands today, a short way from the rocket launch pads of Kourou.

Should a book like Papillon be read as memoir, novel or something in between? And which famous story about a real place do you think bent the truth the most? Tell us in the comments.

videos.title: How the American Mob Secretly Ran an Entire Island Paradise: Havana
videos.description:
What would it take for a gang to run a country without ever holding office? In the last days of 1946, the bosses of the American underworld gathered at the Hotel Nacional in Havana for what was officially a party for Frank Sinatra. What followed was a decade-long partnership between Meyer Lansky's circle and Fulgencio Batista's state: a hotel law with no background checks, public money for casino towers, kickbacks, and a glittering strip of casinos from the Riviera to the Capri. The mob never ran Cuba. It ran the machine that made Cuba a product, and the dictator was always the senior partner. This documentary follows the deal from the Nacional to the night in January 1959 when the slot machines hit the pavement, shows what tourists saw versus what Cubans lived, and ends at the hotel that still stands, where the question of who really won is waiting.

Which part of this story surprised you most: the law that made it possible, the reopening of the casinos after the revolution, or the hotel that still stands? Tell us in the comments, and if you want more stories about paradises and the people who paid for them, subscribe to Paradise Undone.

videos.description:
Three. Three people, a grove of coconut palms and a crooked ribbon of sand: that was all of Cancún on the day the bulldozers arrived in January 1970. Today the same strip holds tens of thousands of hotel rooms, one of the busiest airports in Latin America and a city of almost nine hundred thousand, in a place whose pipes were laid for forty thousand. Did a computer really choose the spot? How do you fill hotels when no investor will build them? And where did the people who built Cancún actually sleep? This is the story of a city drawn in a bank office, financed before it had a single resident, and then overtaken by the people the plan forgot.

videos.title: How Tourists Are Destroying the World's Most Famous Island Right Now: Santorini
videos.description:
Picture the famous sunset at Oia: white walls, a blue dome, a copper sun sinking into a flooded crater, and nobody in the frame but you. Now picture the same corner on a summer day when seven cruise ships arrive together, and thousands of strangers press along a narrow wall filming the same sun. Two months later, the island's own port authority wrote a ceiling into an official decision: never more than eight thousand cruise passengers on the same day. This video argues that when an island's own officials start rationing visitors, building, beds and water, something is being destroyed, and follows the story from the caldera and the Minoan eruption to the donkeys on the steps, the illegal pools, the earthquake winter when the tourists fled, the workers sharing rooms, and the construction freeze that runs out this year. The twist: the island cannot live with the crowd, and it nearly buckled without it.

videos.title: Why Nobody Wants to Visit the Dead Sea Anymore
videos.description:
On the shore of the Dead Sea there is a spa with sulfur pools, mud baths, a restaurant, and a view of nothing. The sea it was built to overlook has walked away, more than a mile, leaving ground full of holes. Some twenty miles south, a hotel strip on the same sea was full enough in late 2023 to shelter hundreds of survivors from a single kibbutz. Both are true at once. This documentary follows the lowest dry land on Earth as its shoreline retreats by roughly a meter a year: who took the water, why the famous hotel strip sits on a salt factory's pond, what the sinkholes and closed beaches say about the shore people came for, how the war has changed who visits in Israel, Jordan and the West Bank, and why the Red Sea to Dead Sea rescue plan never delivered a drop.

Which suspect would you blame most for the fall of the Dead Sea: the diverted river, the evaporation ponds, or the heat? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe to Paradise Undone for more stories about famous places and the fragile systems behind them.

videos.title: The Horrors of Building the Panama Canal
videos.description:
The finest hospital on the Panama isthmus stood the legs of its beds in little dishes of water to keep the ants off the patients. The ants stayed away. The mosquitoes bred in that water instead, and men lay dying of the very fever those insects carried, a few steps from windows with no screens. That one ward opens the story of two attempts to cut a canal through the jungle: the French under Ferdinand de Lesseps, where about twenty-two thousand people are thought to have died, and the American effort, where William Gorgas beat yellow fever and the Culebra Cut still claimed thousands more. This film follows the dynamite blast at Bas Obispo, the landslides that kept refilling the Cut, the official death toll of five thousand six hundred and nine and why it is probably a minimum, what actually killed workers once the mosquito was beaten, and the payroll that divided men into gold and silver, with Barbadian and other West Indian laborers carrying the heaviest risk.

Would you have signed up in nineteen oh seven, knowing the danger? Tell us in the comments what you would have chosen and why. If you want more stories from the places history tried to forget, subscribe to Paradise Undone.

videos.title: he Rise and Fall of Canada's Nickel Capital   Sudbury Ontario
videos.description:
In July 1971, NASA sent Apollo 16 astronauts to train on the pitch-black, lifeless rocks of Sudbury, Ontario—a city so severely scarred by hyper-industrial mining pollution that its toxic terrain genuinely resembled the surface of the Moon.

To understand how a single northern point on the map came to emit more sulphur dioxide than all of modern Europe combined, you have to trace back 1.849 billion years to a massive cosmic impact that shattered the Canadian Shield and deposited the richest nickel basin on Earth.

 For decades, tens of thousands of miners labored beneath a soot-blackened sky, driving an unprecedented economic surge that culminated in the construction of the colossal Inco Superstack—a 381-meter chimney designed to spew millions of tonnes of toxic gas across the continent. 

Sudbury became an invincible titan of global industry, but its blinding prosperity came at a devastating environmental cost.

Yet, when ecological limits were breached and the industrial boom inevitably cracked, losing over sixteen thousand mining jobs, Sudbury did not die.

 Instead of quietly fading into a rust-belt ghost town, this resilient northern community executed one of the most miraculous, paradoxical turnarounds in modern history, defying economic gravity to grow larger and greener than ever before.

videos.title: The Most Impossible Rise of a City Ever   Fort McMurray Alberta
videos.description:
In 2014, a remote industrial outpost carved into the frozen northern subarctic boasted the highest median income in North America and real estate prices that rivaled Vancouver—just nine years later, full condos in the same city were selling for $35,000.

Deep in the northern Alberta muskeg at 56 degrees north—435 kilometers from the nearest major city—built on top of a two-hundred-year-old chemistry problem that experts claimed could never be solved, Fort McMurray defied every law of geographic and economic logic.

 Driven by the massive Athabasca oil sands, this isolated boomtown exploded into a high-octane juggernaut where 21-year-olds commanded 400-tonne haul trucks, local airports moved over a million passengers, and standard suburban homes commanded three-quarters of a million dollars deep inside the Canadian wilderness.

Then came the reckoning: a historic crash in global energy markets, followed immediately by the two most expensive natural disasters in Canadian history, wiping out 60 percent of the region's property value almost overnight. Yet, Fort McMurray’s collapse defied every historical template—it did not wither into a ruined ghost town or leave abandoned streets for the forest to reclaim, remaining a bizarre, high-wage enigma standing tall against the elements. 

This is the cinematic story of the rise, ruin, and unprecedented resilience of North America’s most improbable city.

videos.title: The Rise and Fall of Canada's Most Powerful Company   Hudson's Bay Company
videos.description:
In late 2025, the original 1670 royal charter of a company that once governed a third of North America was sold off at a bankruptcy auction for $18 million. 

The Hudson’s Bay Company didn't collapse from lost wars or failed markets—it spent 162 years slowly dying from a single, catastrophic decision made in a London boardroom in 1863.

Long before Canada was a nation, the Hudson’s Bay Company operated as an unassailable sovereign titan. Wielding its own navy, issuing its own currency, and enforcing its own courts across nearly three million square miles, HBC outlived the Stuart kings and forged an undisputed fur-trading monopoly.

 Yet, behind its vast wilderness fortresses and immense global power lay a silent turning point: a secretive financial deal that surrendered its sovereign territory, rewrote the company's DNA, and initiated the longest, most tragic corporate decline in human history.

Decades later, the inevitable end arrived not on a snowy frontier battlefield, but under the harsh lights of a Toronto auction house. Watch the astonishing rise, fatal miscalculation, and ultimate liquidation of an empire—where forgotten department store calendar prints fetched half a million dollars and King Charles II's sheepskin parchment went under the bankruptcy hammer.

 This is the definitive story of power, greed, and corporate hubris that built—and ultimately dismantled—Canada's most powerful institution.

videos.title: The Rise and Fall of Canada's Most Lawless Boomtown   Dawson City Yukon
videos.description:
On a frozen Yukon mudflat 500 miles from civilization, over 16,000 fortune seekers built North America’s wildest boomtown overnight—a place where single mud lots exploded in value by 800,000% and raw gold dust flowed like water. Yet behind the madness of the Klondike Gold Rush lies a stranger reality: Dawson City began to collapse at the exact moment it hit absolute peak wealth.

In July 1898, red-coated North-West Mounted Police constables conducted a canvas-tent census on a remote subarctic swamp, uncovering a desperate metropolis of over 16,000 people crammed alongside 300 saloons and supply shops. Long before European prospectors arrived, this land at the confluence of the Klondike and Yukon rivers was Tr'ochëk—a sacred salmon fishing camp belonging to the Hän-speaking Tr'ondëk Hwëch'in First Nation. Mispronounced by white traders, the indigenous name meaning "Hammerstone Water" was forever distorted into "Klondike" as gold fever swept the globe, pulling desperate stampeders into an unforgiving wilderness where champagne was bought by the poke and fortunes were won in a single shovelful.

Yet Dawson City’s true epic defies every American Wild West stereotype. Despite its reputation as Canada's most lawless frontier, the boomtown recorded zero murders during its peak frenzy—ruled under the ironclad oversight of the Mounties. videos.title: Why Nobody Wants to Visit Niagara Falls Ontario Anymore
videos.description:
In 2012, over ten million people watched Nik Wallenda walk across the gorge at the absolute peak of Niagara’s global dominance. Today, Canada’s most famous natural wonder has collapsed into a shuttered, overpriced tourist trap that millions of travellers are actively avoiding.

On June 15, 2012, over a hundred thousand spectators crammed the banks of the Niagara Gorge while the golden lights of the Fallsview towers illuminated a town at the summit of world tourism. For over half a century, Niagara Falls, Ontario was the undisputed honeymoon and entertainment capital of Canada—a booming metropolis of mega-casinos, iconic attractions like Marineland, and high-stakes hospitality empires. It was an unstoppable economic force that seemed completely immune to the forces of decay.

Fast-forward to today, and the promenade tells a devastatingly different story. Marineland sits closed and quiet, storefronts along Victoria Avenue are papered over, and American cross-border visitation has plummeted by double digits. Niagara Falls did not collapse from a closed factory or a rerouted highway; it was undone by predatory tourism fees, corporate greed, and a short-sighted business model that chased quick dollars over lasting legacies. This is the tragic story of how a global icon lost its soul, and why tourists are finally turning their backs on Niagara Falls.
